text: PostgreSQL materialized views are not updated automatically: their contents stay as of the last REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW. A plain refresh can block readers; REFRESH ... CONCURRENTLY avoids that but requires a unique index on the view.
why: Readers need to know MVs are stale between refreshes and that refresh can lock reads.

text: Oracle can keep materialized views current automatically (REFRESH FAST ON COMMIT or ON STATEMENT), applying only the changes recorded in materialized view logs instead of recomputing the whole query.
why: Shows that incremental, automatic refresh exists, so it doesn't have to be trigger-based.

text: Linux keeps recently read file data in the page cache (RAM), so a 'disk' cache that is read often is actually served from memory. That is a big part of why a local disk cache can beat a remote cache.
why: Explains the real mechanism behind the disk-cache speedup.

text: On AWS the default root disk is an EBS volume. 'Instance store' disks are physically attached to the host, AWS describes them as ideal for caches and scratch data, and their contents are lost when the instance stops.
why: Clarifies which 'disk' is truly local and what that means for a disk cache.

text: Rough latency orders of magnitude: main-memory reference ~100 ns; random 4 KB SSD read ~150 µs; same-datacenter round trip ~500 µs.
why: Gives readers the numbers behind RAM vs SSD vs network caching decisions.

text: Amazon API Gateway (REST) caches only GET by default, with a default TTL of 300 s (max 3600 s). You can flush a stage's whole cache, and an authorized client can refresh one entry by sending 'Cache-Control: max-age=0'.
why: Corrects the 'only TTL' claim with concrete controls.

text: nginx proxy_cache takes cache lifetime from proxy_cache_valid or from the upstream's X-Accel-Expires / Cache-Control / Expires headers, and by default does not cache responses that set cookies. Purging entries (proxy_cache_purge) is a commercial NGINX Plus feature.
why: Practical detail for anyone caching at the proxy layer.

text: Cloudflare does not cache HTML or JSON by default; to cache API responses at the edge you must add a Cache Rule.
why: Prevents readers assuming a CDN caches API responses out of the box.

text: Mark per-user responses 'Cache-Control: private' so only the browser caches them. Shared caches (CDNs, reverse proxies) may serve anything cacheable to every user.
why: Main safety rule when caching API responses on a CDN.

text: For CDN content that changes, AWS recommends versioned file names over invalidation: users may keep seeing old versions from browser and intermediate caches after an invalidation, and invalidations cost money.
why: A standard cache-busting technique the lecture didn't cover.

text: Redis 6+ supports server-assisted client-side caching (CLIENT TRACKING). Redis remembers which keys a client read and sends it an invalidation message when they change. Redis notes the plain pub/sub approach is costly because invalidations go to every client.
why: Answers the deferred question about keeping API-server caches consistent.

text: Redis's guidance for local caches is to put a maximum TTL on every locally cached key, even if the source key has none, and to cap local cache memory with an eviction policy.
why: Concrete hygiene for the 'TTL and flushing strategy' point.

text: Replica staleness can be measured: on RDS for MySQL the ReplicaLag metric reports Seconds_Behind_Master. With PostgreSQL streaming replication the delay is usually under one second if the standby keeps up.
why: Shows how to measure and reason about replica staleness.

text: MySQL semi-synchronous replication makes a commit wait until at least one replica confirms it has received the events. That ensures committed transactions survive a source crash, but it adds a round trip to each commit, and it falls back to asynchronous if replicas time out.
why: The middle ground between async and sync replication.

text: On Amazon RDS, a Multi-AZ standby is synchronous and takes over automatically but can't serve reads. Read replicas serve reads but must be promoted manually. Aurora promotes a reader automatically, usually in under 60 seconds.
why: Separates high-availability standbys from read-scaling replicas.

text: Built-in read/write routing exists: Aurora's reader endpoint balances connections across replicas, and PostgreSQL's libpq can pick a primary or standby from a host list with target_session_attrs (read-write, standby, prefer-standby).
why: Names the 'magic layers' the lecture mentions.

text: With hash(key) mod N, changing N remaps nearly all keys. Consistent hashing moves only about keys/servers of them on average, which is why shard routers avoid plain modulo.
why: The main sharding pitfall for anyone implementing naive routing.

text: Choose a shard/partition key with many distinct, evenly accessed values (e.g. user ID). Keys with few values or time-bucketed keys (status code, creation date) create hot partitions.
why: Practical guidance where the lecture says there's no formula.

text: RDS for MySQL allows up to 15 read replicas per source, and AWS advises giving each replica the same compute and storage as the source so it can keep up.
why: Puts a real number on replica counts.

text: For spikes you can predict, EC2 Auto Scaling offers predictive scaling (launches capacity ahead of forecast load) and warm pools (pre-initialized stopped instances), so you don't rely on reactive scaling alone.
why: Tools for the 'prepare before the campaign' advice.

text: With ALB sticky sessions, adding many targets can leave load uneven until stickiness is reset. If a target fails, its users are moved to a new target and lose whatever it had cached.
why: The operational cost of sticky-session caching.

text: OWASP: don't store session identifiers in localStorage, because any JavaScript on the page can read it. Use cookies with the HttpOnly flag instead.
why: Security caveat for caching tokens in the browser.

text: localStorage is synchronous and limited to about 5 MiB per origin, and writes past the quota throw QuotaExceededError. MDN recommends IndexedDB for large or performance-sensitive data.
why: Puts numbers on 'a decent amount'.

text: The most common DDoS attacks (UDP reflection, SYN floods) are infrastructure-layer floods that fill network capacity. Mitigating them needs capacity that scales faster than the flood, which application rate limiters don't provide.
why: Corrects 'DDoS = rate limiting'.

text: The transactional outbox pattern writes the outgoing message to the same database, in the same transaction as the business change, then a relay publishes it. It avoids 2PC, which many databases and brokers don't support, at the cost of eventual consistency.
why: The common practical alternative to distributed transactions.
